II-brief-capstone.scenario:
Meridian Health operates hospital groups in Ireland, Illinois, South Korea and Brazil. It is deploying a single AI platform across all four: a triage assistant that ranks emergency arrivals by acuity, plus a generative documentation assistant that drafts clinical notes and patient-facing discharge summaries.

The triage model was built in-house in Dublin. The documentation assistant is a third-party general-purpose model above the systemic-risk threshold, accessed via API, fine-tuned on Meridian's own clinical notes, and deployed under the name "Meridian Scribe". Patient-facing summaries are generated and sent automatically unless a clinician intervenes; clinicians intervene in about 4% of cases.

Meridian's Irish entity is the contracting party for the API. Korean patient data stays in Korea. Illinois staff are also screened for internal promotion using a separate AI tool. Brazilian operations were added by acquisition three months ago and have no AI documentation of any kind. The group CISO has proposed "comply with the EU AI Act everywhere — it's the strictest, so we're covered".

It is September 2026. The board wants a governance position before the platform goes live in November.
II-brief-capstone.fields[0].prompt: Classify each system in each jurisdiction where it operates.
II-brief-capstone.fields[1].prompt: What is Meridian's role for each system, and does it differ by jurisdiction?
II-brief-capstone.fields[2].prompt: Assess the CISO's 'comply with the strictest' proposal.
II-brief-capstone.fields[3].prompt: As of September 2026, which obligations actually bind, and which are still ahead?
II-brief-capstone.fields[4].prompt: What are the three most urgent gaps, and why those three?
II-brief-capstone.fields[5].prompt: State the governance position and the go/no-go recommendation for November.

II-campaign.prompt: Expand your AI company worldwide without running out of compliance capital.

II-case-001.brief: A Dutch insurer licenses a third-party model to price motor policies, retrains it on its own claims history, and markets it to customers under its own brand. Pricing decisions are issued automatically.
II-case-001.steps[0].why: It rebranded the system and substantially modified it by retraining — either alone transfers provider obligations.
II-case-001.steps[1].why: Automatic pricing decisions with significant effects are solely automated decision-making.
II-case-001.steps[2].why: Provider duties for a high-risk system, alongside the DPIA required on the privacy side.

II-case-002.brief: A US retailer's AI screening tool for warehouse roles rejects applicants at a much higher rate from one postal-code cluster that correlates strongly with race. There was no intent to discriminate.
II-case-002.steps[0].why: Facially neutral feature, disproportionate effect, no intent needed.
II-case-002.steps[2].why: The statutory test. "The vendor built it" is not a defence, and overall accuracy does not answer disparate impact.

II-case-003.brief: A board asks why the company should adopt ISO/IEC 42001 when it already intends to comply with the EU AI Act.
II-case-003.steps[0].why: Standards are not law, but a certified management system is strong evidence of the governance the Act demands.
II-case-003.steps[1].why: Certifiability is the practical value; it confers no immunity.

II-case-004.brief: A US company trains a general-purpose model above the systemic-risk compute threshold. It has no EU establishment, but EU businesses integrate the model into their products.
II-case-004.steps[0].why: Extraterritorial reach follows market placement, not establishment.
II-case-004.steps[1].why: Systemic-risk duties sit on top of the baseline GPAI set.
II-case-004.steps[2].why: Third-country GPAI providers must appoint an EU authorised representative.

II-case-005.brief: A marketing agency fine-tunes an LLM on scraped web content to generate campaign copy. Some source sites carry machine-readable rights reservations. The campaign targets construction businesses, not individuals.
II-case-005.steps[0].why: The commercial exception can be reserved; the research exception cannot.
II-case-005.steps[1].why: Legal persons are outside GDPR, but named individuals at those firms are personal data.

II-case-006.brief: It is September 2026. Your board asks which EU AI Act obligations currently bind the company's Annex III recruitment system.
II-case-006.steps[0].why: Prohibitions since February 2025, transparency since August 2026; high-risk deferred to December 2027.
II-case-006.steps[1].why: A deferral is not a repeal, and conformity work takes longer than the extension granted.

II-map-jurisdictions.prompt: Match each instrument to its jurisdiction, then answer what actually binds you there.
II-map-jurisdictions.note: Positions are the real coordinates of each jurisdiction, projected onto a Miller-style world map. Labels for dense regions are nudged clear of their marker; the marker itself is always at the true location.
II-map-jurisdictions.legend[0].label: Comprehensive AI law in force
II-map-jurisdictions.legend[1].label: Sectoral or partial rules in force
II-map-jurisdictions.legend[2].label: Voluntary or non-binding framework
II-map-jurisdictions.legend[3].label: Proposed, not in force
II-map-jurisdictions.legend[4].label: No AI-specific statute
II-map-jurisdictions.legend[5].label: Binding treaty — binds states, not companies
II-map-jurisdictions.projection.note: x/y are computed at build time from lat/lon by tools/build_aigp_game.py

II-roles.prompt: Assign each obligation to the role it attaches to. Obligations follow actors, not systems.

II-timeline-global.prompt: Place each milestone on the timeline, then answer: on a given date, which obligations actually bind you?
II-timeline-global.note: Jurisdictions marked scope "horizon" are professional currency rather than blueprint content; they are excluded from mastery scoring. "Ongoing / uncertain" covers proposed bills and rolling state/regional developments with no confirmed date.

II.A-brief-01.scenario:
Helio, a SaaS company headquartered in Berlin, has eleven years of customer support transcripts — roughly 40 million messages. Customers were told at collection that the data would be used to "resolve your support request and improve our service". Helio's new product team wants to fine-tune a language model on the full archive to build an automated support agent, and later to license that agent to other companies.

The archive is not clean. Customers routinely paste screenshots, order numbers, and occasionally health information when explaining why they missed a payment. About 12% of transcripts come from users who have since closed their accounts, and 3% from users who have made erasure requests that were actioned against the account record but not against the transcript store. The transcripts are stored in Frankfurt, but the fine-tuning would run on infrastructure in Oregon.

The product team's position is that the transcripts are Helio's own business records, that "improve our service" covers building a better support agent, and that because the model will not reproduce transcripts verbatim, no personal data leaves the training process. The general counsel is uneasy but cannot articulate why. You are asked for a written position before the sprint starts.
II.A-brief-01.fields[0].prompt: Is "improve our service" a sufficient basis for this training, and for the licensing plan?
II.A-brief-01.fields[0].hint: Address purpose limitation and compatibility separately for each of the two uses.
II.A-brief-01.fields[1].prompt: How do you handle the closed accounts and the 3% erasure requests?
II.A-brief-01.fields[2].prompt: What follows from the incidental health information in the transcripts?
II.A-brief-01.fields[3].prompt: What does the Frankfurt-to-Oregon training run require?
II.A-brief-01.fields[4].prompt: What controls and documentation would you require before the sprint starts?
II.A-brief-01.fields[5].prompt: State your position to the general counsel in five sentences or fewer.

II.A-pair-009.a.text: A lender declines a loan automatically on the model score, with no human review.
II.A-pair-009.a.why: A decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects triggers Art. 22 safeguards.
II.A-pair-009.b.text: The model flags the application and an underwriter reviews the file and can overturn it.
II.A-pair-009.b.why: Meaningful human involvement with real authority to change the outcome takes it outside "solely" automated. Rubber-stamping does not count.

II.A-pair-010.a.text: A system processes facial images specifically to identify a named individual.
II.A-pair-010.a.why: Biometric data processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person is special-category data.
II.A-pair-010.b.text: A system processes facial images only to count how many people are in a room.
II.A-pair-010.b.why: Without the identification purpose the same raw data is not Art. 9 biometric data, though it remains personal data.

II.A-pair-011.a.text: Customer service transcripts collected to resolve tickets are reused to train a commercial model.
II.A-pair-011.a.why: Training a product on data collected for support is not what the data subject was told; it needs a fresh basis or genuine compatibility analysis.
II.A-pair-011.b.text: The same transcripts are used to audit whether ticket resolution met the stated service standard.
II.A-pair-011.b.why: Quality assurance of the very service the data was collected for is a compatible further purpose.

II.A-pair-012.a.text: A model infers users' likely religious beliefs from their posting history.
II.A-pair-012.a.why: Inferring a special category attribute is processing that category, even though it was never collected directly.
II.A-pair-012.b.text: A model records which product pages each user visited.
II.A-pair-012.b.why: Behavioural data alone is personal but not special category, unless it is used to infer a protected attribute.

II.A-tell-009.snippet: The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them.
II.A-tell-009.tell: "solely on automated processing" plus "legal effects or similarly significantly affects" is Art. 22. It is a data-protection right, not an AI Act obligation — a favourite exam trap.

II.A-tell-010.snippet: Where a type of processing … is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data.
II.A-tell-010.tell: "rights and freedoms of natural persons" plus "prior to the processing" is the GDPR DPIA. Distinguish from the AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment and from ISO 42005 guidance.

II.B-brief-01.scenario:
Marchetti Logistics runs 400 warehouses across the United States and hires around 30,000 seasonal staff each year. To cope, it has deployed a third-party AI screening tool that scores applicants on a 0–100 "reliability index" built from work history, commute distance, prior seasonal completion rates, and a short situational judgement questionnaire. Anyone below 55 is auto-rejected without human review. The vendor describes the model as "bias-tested and EEOC-aligned" but will not disclose the feature weights, calling them proprietary.

Six months in, an internal analyst notices that applicants from three postal-code clusters are rejected at roughly 2.4 times the rate of others. Those clusters are predominantly Black and Hispanic. Commute distance is by far the heaviest-weighted feature. Separately, the tool has been marketed to Marchetti's own clients as a service, and Marchetti's website advertises it as "removing human bias from hiring".

Marchetti's operations director argues that commute distance is a legitimate business factor because long commutes predict no-shows, that the vendor certified the tool, and that no protected characteristic is used as an input. The head of HR wants to keep using it through peak season and review afterwards. You are the AI governance lead.
II.B-brief-01.fields[0].prompt: What is the legal exposure, and under which statutes?
II.B-brief-01.fields[1].prompt: Is "commute distance predicts no-shows" a valid defence? Reason it through.
II.B-brief-01.fields[2].prompt: What is the significance of the vendor's certification and refusal to disclose weights?
II.B-brief-01.fields[3].prompt: Does the "removes human bias" claim create separate exposure?
II.B-brief-01.fields[4].prompt: Respond to the proposal to keep using it through peak season.
II.B-brief-01.fields[5].prompt: What would you require, in what order, and on what timescale?

II.B-pair-013.a.text: A hiring model is deliberately configured to downweight applicants from a protected group.
II.B-pair-013.a.why: Intentional differential treatment on a protected characteristic.
II.B-pair-013.b.text: A hiring model uses postal code, which correlates strongly with race, and rejects one group at a far higher rate.
II.B-pair-013.b.why: Facially neutral feature, disproportionate effect, no intent required. Proxy variables are the classic AI exposure.

II.B-pair-014.a.text: An AI tool screens candidates for a warehouse role and disadvantages older applicants.
II.B-pair-014.a.why: Employment discrimination sits under Title VII, with the ADEA covering age specifically.
II.B-pair-014.b.text: An AI model sets credit limits and produces systematically lower limits for one protected group.
II.B-pair-014.b.why: Credit decisions fall under ECOA, which also requires specific adverse action reasons — hard to give from an opaque model.

II.B-pair-015.a.text: A vendor advertises 99% accuracy for its AI screening tool without evidence.
II.B-pair-015.a.why: Unsubstantiated performance claims are deceptive practices under FTC Act §5.
II.B-pair-015.b.text: A firmware update to an AI home robot causes erratic movement that damages property.
II.B-pair-015.b.why: Defect causing damage is product liability; the EU's revised regime expressly brings software and AI within scope.

II.B-pair-016.a.text: A company scrapes news sites commercially where publishers have machine-readably reserved their rights.
II.B-pair-016.a.why: The EU commercial TDM exception can be opted out of by an express reservation, so scraping needs a licence.
II.B-pair-016.b.text: A university mines the same corpus for non-commercial scientific research with lawful access.
II.B-pair-016.b.why: The research TDM exception cannot be overridden by contract or reservation.

II.B-tell-011.snippet: Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce are hereby declared unlawful.
II.B-tell-011.tell: "unfair or deceptive acts or practices" is the literal statutory phrase of FTC Act §5 — the main US hook for overstated AI capability claims.

II.B-tell-012.snippet: A practice that is neutral on its face but falls more harshly on a protected group, and which cannot be justified by business necessity.
II.B-tell-012.tell: "Neutral on its face" plus "business necessity" is the disparate-impact test. Disparate treatment needs intent; disparate impact does not — which is why proxy features in a model are the usual AI exposure.

II.C-amend-001.a.text: The AI Act lists 8 distinct prohibited AI practices under Article 5 — no specific rule against synthetic intimate imagery.
II.C-amend-001.a.why: The original Article 5 list of 8 practices predates the Amendments Regulation.
II.C-amend-001.b.text: Article 5 prohibits AI systems intended to generate or manipulate non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM, including systems with inadequate safety guardrails, alongside the original 8 practices.
II.C-amend-001.b.why: The Amendments Regulation adds this ninth prohibited practice, closing a gap the original 8-item list left open.

II.C-amend-002.a.text: A provider whose system meets the Article 6(3) derogation criteria (exempted from high-risk classification) must register it in the EU's public database, providing full supporting information.
II.C-amend-002.a.why: The original Article 6(3)/71 registration duty requires the full information set for these exempted systems.
II.C-amend-002.b.text: An exempted system under Article 6(3) is registered in the EU's public database with a reduced information set.
II.C-amend-002.b.why: The Amendments Regulation keeps the registration duty but reduces the information burden for exempted systems.

II.C-amend-003.a.text: Providers and deployers are required to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff.
II.C-amend-003.a.why: Article 4's original wording is a duty to ensure literacy outright.
II.C-amend-003.b.text: Providers and deployers are required to support the development of AI literacy of their staff.
II.C-amend-003.b.why: The Amendments Regulation softens Article 4 from an 'ensure' duty to a 'support the development of' duty.

II.C-amend-004.a.text: Only high-risk AI system providers may process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction, and only when strictly necessary with safeguards in place.
II.C-amend-004.a.why: The original Article 10(5) scope is limited to high-risk AI system providers.
II.C-amend-004.b.text: Providers and deployers of other AI systems and GPAI models, and deployers of high-risk AI systems, may process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction when strictly necessary with safeguards in place.
II.C-amend-004.b.why: The Amendments Regulation widens Article 10(5)'s scope beyond just high-risk providers, while keeping the strict-necessity/safeguards test unchanged.

II.C-amend-005.a.text: The European AI Office and member state regulators have overlapping regulatory powers for AI systems built on GPAI models, where the same provider developed both the model and the system.
II.C-amend-005.a.why: The original allocation of powers between the AI Office and national regulators is overlapping, not exclusive.
II.C-amend-005.b.text: The European AI Office has exclusive competence over AI systems built on GPAI models where the same provider developed both — except for high-risk systems under Annex I and specific Annex III categories such as critical infrastructure and law enforcement.
II.C-amend-005.b.why: The Amendments Regulation moves the AI Office from overlapping to exclusive competence for this category, carving out Annex I and specific Annex III high-risk systems.

II.C-amend-006.a.text: Enforcement penalties are capped for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), but small mid-cap (SMC) enterprises get no such cap.
II.C-amend-006.a.why: The original penalty regime's proportionality cap applies to SMEs only.
II.C-amend-006.b.text: SMEs and SMCs pay the lower of the percentage of global annual turnover or the fixed amount, while larger organisations pay the higher value.
II.C-amend-006.b.why: The Amendments Regulation extends the SME proportionality cap to SMCs on the same lower-of-two-values basis.

II.C-amend-007.a.text: AI systems that are products, or safety components of products, regulated by the EU Machinery Regulation must directly adhere to the AI Act's high-risk AI system requirements.
II.C-amend-007.a.why: In the original Annex I, the Machinery Regulation sits in Section A, which triggers direct high-risk AI Act requirements.
II.C-amend-007.b.text: The Machinery Regulation sits in Annex I Section B, so the AI Act's high-risk AI system requirements do not apply to it directly.
II.C-amend-007.b.why: The Amendments Regulation reclassifies the Machinery Regulation into Annex I Section B, removing the direct high-risk trigger.

II.C-brief-01.scenario:
NordBank, headquartered in Stockholm, licenses a general-purpose model from a US developer with no EU establishment. NordBank fine-tunes the model on twelve years of its own customer transaction data, wraps it in a decisioning layer, and deploys it to make consumer credit decisions across the Nordics and Germany. It is marketed to customers as "NordBank AI Advisor". Declines under €10,000 are issued automatically; above that, a credit officer reviews a one-line summary and, in practice, follows the recommendation 97% of the time.

The US developer's model was trained above the systemic-risk compute threshold. NordBank's contract with the developer disclaims all liability for downstream use and provides no technical documentation beyond a public model card. NordBank has not performed a conformity assessment; its position is that it is "only a customer" of the model. It plans to offer the Advisor to two smaller partner banks next year.

A declined customer has asked, in writing, how the decision about her was reached and what data was used. The board wants to know its exposure before the partner-bank rollout.
II.C-brief-01.fields[0].prompt: What is NordBank under the EU AI Act, and what is the US developer? Justify each.
II.C-brief-01.fields[1].prompt: What is the risk classification of the Advisor, and on what basis?
II.C-brief-01.fields[2].prompt: Which obligations attach to NordBank, and which to the developer?
II.C-brief-01.fields[3].prompt: Which other regimes are engaged, and what do they require here?
II.C-brief-01.fields[4].prompt: How must NordBank answer the declined customer?
II.C-brief-01.fields[5].prompt: Quantify the exposure and state what must happen before the partner-bank rollout.

II.C-ladder-penalties.prompt: Order these breaches from the highest maximum penalty to the lowest.
II.C-ladder-penalties.steps[0].label: Breach of the Article 5 prohibitions
II.C-ladder-penalties.steps[0].detail: Up to €35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
II.C-ladder-penalties.steps[1].label: Non-compliance with other obligations
II.C-ladder-penalties.steps[1].detail: Up to €15 million or 3% — provider and deployer duties, notified body and transparency obligations.
II.C-ladder-penalties.steps[2].label: Supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities

II.C-ladder-phases.prompt: Order the EU AI Act milestones from earliest to latest.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[0].label: Entry into force
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[0].detail: The Act enters into force; obligations phase in afterwards.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[1].label: Prohibitions and AI literacy
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[1].detail: Article 5 prohibited practices and Article 4 AI literacy duties apply.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[2].label: GPAI obligations and governance
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[2].detail: General-purpose AI model obligations, governance bodies and most penalty provisions apply.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[3].label: Article 50 transparency
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[3].detail: Transparency duties for AI interaction, synthetic content, deepfakes and emotion recognition. Unchanged by the Omnibus.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[4].label: High-risk: standalone Annex III
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[4].detail: Employment, credit, education, essential services and similar. Deferred roughly 16 months.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[5].label: GPAI models placed before Aug 2025
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[5].detail: Legacy general-purpose models must reach compliance.
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[6].label: High-risk: Annex I embedded products
II.C-ladder-phases.steps[6].detail: AI inside regulated products under existing sectoral law. Deferred 12 months.

II.C-pair-001.a.text: An AI system screens job applicants and produces a ranked shortlist that recruiters hire from.
II.C-pair-001.a.why: Annex III employment use — the system materially influences who gets hired.
II.C-pair-001.b.text: The same system only sorts applicants alphabetically for a recruiter who reads every CV and decides independently.
II.C-pair-001.b.why: Art. 6(3): a narrow procedural task that does not materially influence the outcome falls outside high-risk.

II.C-pair-002.a.text: A bank licenses a third-party high-risk model and uses it internally under the vendor's brand.
II.C-pair-002.a.why: Using a system under another's name keeps you a deployer.
II.C-pair-002.b.text: The same bank puts its own trademark on the system and offers it to customers as its own.
II.C-pair-002.b.why: Placing your name or trademark on a high-risk system makes you its provider, with the full provider obligation set.

II.C-pair-003.a.text: Police run real-time remote biometric identification across a public square to find suspects generally.
II.C-pair-003.a.why: Art. 5 bans real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, save narrow authorised exceptions.
II.C-pair-003.b.text: Police run the same biometric matching after the fact, on stored footage, under judicial authorisation.
II.C-pair-003.b.why: Post-remote biometric identification is not banned but is Annex III high-risk with authorisation requirements.

II.C-pair-004.a.text: An employer deploys emotion recognition to monitor staff attentiveness at their desks.
II.C-pair-004.a.why: Art. 5 bans emotion inference in the workplace and in education, outside medical and safety uses.
II.C-pair-004.b.text: A games studio uses emotion recognition in a consumer entertainment app, disclosed to the user.
II.C-pair-004.b.why: Outside workplace and education the ban does not bite; Art. 50 transparency duties apply instead.

II.C-pair-005.a.text: A provider releases a general-purpose model trained well below the systemic-risk compute threshold.
II.C-pair-005.a.why: Baseline duties: technical documentation, information to downstream providers, copyright policy, training-data summary.
II.C-pair-005.b.text: The same provider releases a model whose cumulative training compute exceeds the systemic-risk threshold.
II.C-pair-005.b.why: Adds model evaluation, adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity duties.

II.C-pair-006.a.text: An organisation deploys a prohibited social-scoring system.
II.C-pair-006.a.why: Breach of the Art. 5 prohibitions attracts the top band.
II.C-pair-006.b.text: An organisation deploys a high-risk system but fails to keep the required technical documentation.
II.C-pair-006.b.why: Non-compliance with obligations other than the Art. 5 prohibitions sits in the middle band.

II.C-pair-007.a.text: A hospital uses a CE-marked diagnostic AI exactly as the vendor intended.
II.C-pair-007.a.why: Use within the intended purpose leaves provider duties with the vendor.
II.C-pair-007.b.text: The hospital retrains the model on its own data and applies it to a different clinical purpose.
II.C-pair-007.b.why: A substantial modification, or a change of intended purpose that makes a system high-risk, transfers provider obligations to you.

II.C-pair-008.a.text: A Dublin firm brings a US-built high-risk system into the EU market for the first time.
II.C-pair-008.a.why: Placing a third-country system on the EU market makes you the importer: verify conformity assessment, CE marking, documentation and the authorised representative.
II.C-pair-008.b.text: A Dublin firm resells that system onward within the EU without altering it.
II.C-pair-008.b.why: Distributors make available a system already on the market; duties are lighter but include checking CE marking and not supplying a system they know to be non-compliant.

II.C-pair-019.a.text: As the AI Act was originally enacted, when did obligations for standalone Annex III high-risk systems apply?
II.C-pair-019.a.why: The original two-year phase-in date, and what the study guide teaches.
II.C-pair-019.b.text: After the Digital Omnibus agreed in May 2026, when do those same obligations apply?
II.C-pair-019.b.why: The Omnibus deferred standalone Annex III obligations by roughly 16 months. Annex I embedded systems moved to 2 August 2028.

II.C-pair-020.a.text: A chatbot must be built so that users can tell they are interacting with an AI system.
II.C-pair-020.a.why: Art. 50 places design-time disclosure for AI interaction on the provider.
II.C-pair-020.b.text: An employer using an emotion recognition system must inform the people exposed to it.
II.C-pair-020.b.why: Art. 50 places the duty to inform exposed individuals on the deployer operating the system.

II.C-tell-007.snippet: Providers shall ensure that the system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure prior to its placing on the market, and shall draw up an EU declaration of conformity.
II.C-tell-007.tell: "shall" plus conformity assessment, declaration of conformity and placing on the market is EU product-safety legislation. Standards never say "shall … prior to placing on the market".

II.D-brief-01.scenario:
You have joined a 900-person medical devices company as its first AI governance lead. The company builds imaging software with embedded AI, sold in the EU and the US. It already holds ISO 13485 and ISO 27001 certification and has a mature quality management system.

The CTO wants to "adopt the NIST AI RMF because it's free and the Americans use it". The quality director wants ISO/IEC 42001 "because we can certify it and our auditors already know ISO". The general counsel says neither matters because "only the EU AI Act is law". The CEO has asked for a one-page recommendation and is impatient with nuance.

Complicating this: the company's products are Annex I embedded AI under the EU AI Act, not standalone Annex III. Nobody in the room knows what that changes. The board also wants to state something about responsible AI in the annual report and has asked whether the company can say it "complies with the OECD AI Principles".
II.D-brief-01.fields[0].prompt: Explain the relationship between the AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the OECD Principles.
II.D-brief-01.fields[1].prompt: Is the general counsel right that only the AI Act matters?
II.D-brief-01.fields[2].prompt: What does being Annex I embedded rather than Annex III change?
II.D-brief-01.fields[3].prompt: Which ISO standards are relevant here, and what does each actually do?
II.D-brief-01.fields[4].prompt: Can the company claim it 'complies with the OECD AI Principles'?
II.D-brief-01.fields[5].prompt: Give the one-page recommendation the CEO asked for.

II.D-pair-017.a.text: An organisation fails to complete a conformity assessment for a high-risk AI system.
II.D-pair-017.a.why: EU AI Act obligation, enforceable with administrative fines.
II.D-pair-017.b.text: An organisation chooses not to implement the NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function.
II.D-pair-017.b.why: The AI RMF is voluntary guidance. It carries no penalty — though it may inform what counts as reasonable practice.

II.D-pair-018.a.text: An organisation seeks third-party certification of its AI governance arrangements.
II.D-pair-018.a.why: ISO/IEC 42001 is a management system standard, so it can be audited and certified against.
II.D-pair-018.b.text: An organisation wants agreed definitions of "AI system" and "machine learning" for its policy set.
II.D-pair-018.b.why: ISO/IEC 22989 supplies vocabulary and concepts; there is nothing to certify against.

II.D-tell-001.snippet: The organization shall establish, implement, maintain and continually improve an AI management system, including the processes needed and their interactions.
II.D-tell-001.tell: "management system" plus the "establish, implement, maintain and continually improve" formula is ISO management-standard boilerplate. It is the same sentence shape as ISO 27001 and 9001.

II.D-tell-002.snippet: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE are the four core functions, each broken into categories and subcategories.
II.D-tell-002.tell: Four verbs in capitals is unique to NIST. Nothing else in Domain II organises itself into GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE.

II.D-tell-003.snippet: This document provides a vocabulary and describes concepts and terminology for AI, so that different communities can use consistent language.
II.D-tell-003.tell: Vocabulary and concepts only, with nothing to certify against, is 22989. If a standard tells you what words mean rather than what to do, it is the terminology standard.

II.D-tell-004.snippet: Guidance on the process for performing an impact assessment of an AI system on individuals and societies.
II.D-tell-004.tell: Impact assessment process = 42005. Easily confused with 42001 (the management system) and 23894 (risk management). BoK v2.1 names 22989, 42001 and 42005 as the three core ISO standards.

II.D-tell-005.snippet: AI actors should respect the rule of law, human rights and democratic values throughout the AI system lifecycle, including inclusive growth and sustainable development.
II.D-tell-005.tell: OECD wording shows in the phrase "AI actors" combined with talk of well-being and of growth that is inclusive and sustainable. The text sets out values rather than duties, and it speaks to governments as much as to companies.

II.D-tell-006.snippet: An evaluation programme that assesses model performance in laboratory, in controlled field testing, and in real-world use, in three layers.
II.D-tell-006.tell: Layered evaluation moving from lab to field to real world is ARIA (Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI). The AI RMF is a framework; ARIA is a testing programme that feeds it.

II.D-tell-008.snippet: A companion resource offering suggested actions, references and documentation for each subcategory, which organisations may use in whole or in part.
II.D-tell-008.tell: "Suggested actions" that are voluntary and per-subcategory is the Playbook, the companion to the AI RMF. BoK II.D.2 names the Playbook alongside the framework.

authrep.definition: Appointed in writing by a third-country provider to act on its behalf in the EU.

controller.definition: Determines the purposes and means of processing.

deployer.definition: Uses an AI system under its own authority, other than in a personal non-professional activity.

distributor.definition: Makes a system available on the EU market without being provider or importer.

dpo.definition: Appointed to inform, advise and monitor compliance, independently.

gdpr-rep.definition: Represents a non-EU controller or processor within the EU.

grid-eu-amend-01.original.text: The AI Act lists 8 distinct prohibited AI practices under Article 5 — no specific rule against synthetic intimate imagery.
grid-eu-amend-01.updated.text: Article 5 prohibits AI systems intended to generate or manipulate non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM, including systems with inadequate safety guardrails, alongside the original 8 practices.

grid-eu-amend-02.original.text: Applicable date is 2 August 2026 (for Annex III AI systems) and 2 August 2027 (for Annex I AI systems).
grid-eu-amend-02.updated.text: Applicable date is postponed to 2 December 2027 (for Annex III AI systems) and 2 August 2028 (for Annex I AI systems).

grid-eu-amend-03.original.text: All Article 50 obligations apply from 2 August 2026. This includes the AI output detection and watermarking obligation (Article 50(2)).
grid-eu-amend-03.updated.text: Applicable date for the AI output detection and watermarking obligation (Article 50(2)) postponed to 2 December 2026, for legacy AI systems only.

grid-eu-amend-04.original.text: A provider whose system meets the Article 6(3) derogation criteria (exempted from high-risk classification) must register it in the EU's public database, providing full supporting information.
grid-eu-amend-04.updated.text: An exempted system under Article 6(3) is registered in the EU's public database with a reduced information set.

grid-eu-amend-05.original.text: Providers and deployers are required to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff.
grid-eu-amend-05.updated.text: Providers and deployers are required to support the development of AI literacy of their staff.

grid-eu-amend-06.original.text: Only high-risk AI system providers may process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction, and only when strictly necessary with safeguards in place.
grid-eu-amend-06.updated.text: Providers and deployers of other AI systems and GPAI models, and deployers of high-risk AI systems, may process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction when strictly necessary with safeguards in place.

grid-eu-amend-07.original.text: The European AI Office and member state regulators have overlapping regulatory powers for AI systems built on GPAI models, where the same provider developed both the model and the system.
grid-eu-amend-07.updated.text: The European AI Office has exclusive competence over AI systems built on GPAI models where the same provider developed both — except for high-risk systems under Annex I and specific Annex III categories such as critical infrastructure and law enforcement.

grid-eu-amend-08.original.text: Enforcement penalties are capped for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), but small mid-cap (SMC) enterprises get no such cap.
grid-eu-amend-08.updated.text: SMEs and SMCs pay the lower of the percentage of global annual turnover or the fixed amount, while larger organisations pay the higher value.

grid-eu-amend-09.original.text: AI systems that are products, or safety components of products, regulated by the EU Machinery Regulation must directly adhere to the AI Act's high-risk AI system requirements.
grid-eu-amend-09.updated.text: The Machinery Regulation sits in Annex I Section B, so the AI Act's high-risk AI system requirements do not apply to it directly.

ii-rr-ae-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — there is no nationwide AI-specific banking duty; the binding instrument is DIFC Regulation 10 inside the zone, and even ADGM next door has only guidance, no Regulation-10 equivalent. (c) fails because the Charter binds no one.

ii-rr-ae-n01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — CE marking and declarations of conformity are EU AI Act artifacts with no DIFC counterpart. (c) is NYC Local Law 144's employer duty. Regulation 10 asks for the data-protection-style cluster, with fines around USD 25k–50k per violation.

ii-rr-ae-n02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): January 2026 changed enforcement intensity, not geography — Regulation 10 binds only within the DIFC. The Charter (c) has no enforcement chapter. Mainland processing answers to PDPL (Decree-Law 45/2021), with a reported 2027-01-01 compliance deadline.

ii-rr-ae-s01.why: The nearest confusable is (b): no horizontal UAE AI statute exists — the June 2026 federal body is a regulator, not an act. (c) inverts the Charter, which is aspirational. (d) ignores that one binding instrument does exist, but only inside the financial free zone.

ii-rr-ae-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — regulator is not statute: the 2026-06-14 announcement created the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, while the UAE still has no horizontal AI law. (c) is wrong because Regulation 10 stays scoped to the DIFC free zone.

ii-rr-ae-s03.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the instrument with real fines (about USD 25k–50k per violation) is DIFC Regulation 10, not the Charter (July 2024), which has no enforcement arm. (d) invents a repeal — the Charter simply sits alongside the new authority.

ii-rr-any-k01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): ISO/IEC 42005 is GUIDANCE for AI impact assessments — not a management-system standard and not certifiable. (c) — the NIST AI RMF is voluntary with no certification scheme behind it; (d) — CE marking attests a PRODUCT'S conformity, never an organisation's governance.

ii-rr-any-n01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): modification is a SEPARATE trigger (Art. 25(1)(b)) — name-or-trademark substitution alone re-allocates the provider role under Art. 25(1)(a). (c) mistakes the supply-chain geography test for the branding test; (d) invents a sharing rule the Act does not contain.

ii-rr-any-n02.why: Nearest confusable is (b): putting a substantially modified high-risk system INTO SERVICE under your own authority triggers the Art. 25(1)(b) shift even without a sale. (c) is wrong on the residue — the original provider owes cooperation and documentation handover, not responsibility for someone else's modification.

ii-rr-any-n03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the vendor's INTENDED PURPOSE fixed the original classification — whoever changes that purpose so the system becomes high-risk takes the provider role for the new use (Art. 25(1)(c)). (c) would leave a high-risk use ungoverned, which the role-shift rule exists to prevent.

ii-rr-any-n04.why: Nearest confusable is (b): releasing a modified model under your own name is provider activity, not use — the Commission's GPAI guidelines treat significant fine-tunes as making you provider OF THE MODIFICATION, while the upstream lab keeps duties for the base model (contra c). (d) invents an AI Act licensing rule; that question is contract and IP law.

ii-rr-any-n05.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Art. 25(2) keeps the initial provider on the hook for cooperation, information and reasonable technical access. But it does not make it a co-assessor of a system it no longer controls (c) — the conformity duty travels whole to the new provider.

ii-rr-any-n06.why: Scale of use is not a trigger — the nearest confusable is assuming heavy operational reliance alone converts a deployer. The three statutory triggers are exactly (b), (c) and (d): rebranding, substantial modification, and purpose change into high-risk (Art. 25(1)(a)–(c)).

ii-rr-any-w01.why: Nearest confusable is (c): 'binding statute' does not mean 'business duties' — Japan's Act No. 53 of 2025 is binding law addressed to the STATE, with a deliberate no-penalty design, while Korea's Act No. 20676 (in force 2026-01-22) imposes operator duties, softened only by MSIT's 2026 enforcement grace period.

ii-rr-any-w02.why: Nearest confusable is (c), the retained-EU-law reflex: the AI Act post-dates Brexit and never applied in the UK. (d) fails on currency — the EU's prohibitions, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency are already live; only the high-risk regime waits until 2027-12-02.

ii-rr-any-w03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) NEVER took effect — delayed, challenged in court by xAI with DOJ intervening, then repealed and replaced by SB 26-189 (signed 2026-05-14, effective 2027-01-01). Texas's HB 149 has been enforceable by the AG since New Year 2026.

ii-rr-any-w04.why: Nearest confusable is (d), the clean inversion: a REGULATION has direct effect on operators across member states, while a TREATY obliges its state parties to act. Mixing up which instrument works which way is the exact error this pairing punishes.

ii-rr-any-w05.why: Nearest confusable is (b): 'Brussels effect' logic predicts convergence, but the February 2025 Federal Council decision expressly rejected a horizontal act. The catch for Swiss firms: the EU AI Act still reaches them extraterritorially whenever their systems' output is used in the EU.

ii-rr-any-w06.why: Nearest confusable is (b): AIDA died with Parliament's prorogation and was never revived — Canada's 2023 generative-AI code remains voluntary. (c) fails on status: PL 2338 is still a bill before Brazil's legislature. Korea's Act No. 20676 has been in force since 2026-01-22.

ii-rr-any-w07.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Digital Omnibus deferral hit the ANNEX III high-risk duties, not Article 50, which became enforceable on 2026-08-02. (c) is stale — Korea's Act has been in force since January 2026; (d) borrows the litigation story from COLORADO (xAI/DOJ v. the old SB 24-205) and pins it on the wrong state.

ii-rr-au-c01.why: This government-internal DTA policy is the confusable that fuels 'Australia went mandatory' claims — it binds federal agencies as an administrative policy, while the private sector remains under voluntary guidance and general law. Note the date discipline: agency full compliance is 2026-12-15, distinct from the Privacy Act ADM date in December 2026.

ii-rr-au-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the abandoned proposal — the December 2026 change comes from the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024, existing law adapting to AI, not an AI statute. The AI Safety Institute stays advisory; it gained no powers.

ii-rr-au-k01.why: The adviser is working from stale 2024 reporting on the proposals paper. The only binding accents in Australia are government-internal agency rules (from 2026-06-15) and the Privacy Act ADM transparency change (December 2026) — neither is 'AI guardrails', and neither touches ordinary private-sector deployment.

ii-rr-au-s01.why: The nearest confusable is (d): the Commonwealth-agency requirements ARE binding (first requirements 2026-06-15) but only on federal agencies, never on the private sector. (b) and (c) never happened — the guidance stack stayed voluntary (the AI6 Guidance for AI Adoption superseded the 2024 standard in October 2025) and no AI act exists.

ii-rr-au-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the stale-news trap: 2024 reporting made mandatory guardrails look inevitable, but the National AI Plan formally dropped them. The Australian AI Safety Institute (launched early 2026, AUD 29.9m) is advisory, not a regulator — no enforcement powers came with it.

ii-rr-br-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the design builds on the EXISTING authority rather than replacing it: the ANPD is tipped as coordinator of the SIA, with sector regulators retained. Fragmented state-level enforcement (c) is the US pattern, not the bill's.

ii-rr-br-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the Senate already approved the bill in 2024; the pending step is the Chamber, and the scheduled 27 May 2026 vote simply never happened. Archiving (c) would require a floor defeat that never occurred; the bill remains live in committee.

ii-rr-br-k01.why: The nearest confusable is (c), which mistakes bicameral progress for enactment — Senate approval in 2024 created no duties; the Chamber has not voted. Retroactive application (b) is not how the bill is drafted. Budget goes to the LGPD obligations that bind now.

ii-rr-br-s01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the Latin American framework actually in force since January 2026 is PERU's, not Brazil's. PL 2338/2023 passed the Senate on 2024-12-10 and sits 'Aguardando Parecer' in the Chamber; there has been no floor vote, veto or withdrawal.

ii-rr-br-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (d) — the ANPD is tipped to coordinate the bill's future enforcement system, but it has issued no binding AI-role duties; contracting as if the bill were law imports obligations that do not exist. The role names themselves are correctly Brazilian (b is wrong): the bill does not copy EU labels.

ii-rr-br-s03.why: The nearest confusable is (d), the legal-vacuum myth — no AI act does not mean no law; the LGPD's Article 20 already gives review rights over automated decisions. Provisional application (b) is not a thing in Brazilian legislative procedure, and the EU AI Act (c) reaches EU-market conduct, not domestic Brazilian processing.

ii-rr-ca-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — code signatories make voluntary commitments, which is the opposite of binding law. The ADM Directive binds government deployers only; a federally REGULATED private company (banks, airlines) is still outside its scope, which trips up option (b) thinkers.

ii-rr-ca-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the 'AI for All' strategy (launched 2026-06-04) and the February 2026 consultation summary signal rules on safety testing and oversight to come, but nothing has been tabled. Option (c) is a category error — the EU AI Act has no accession mechanism for states.

ii-rr-ca-k01.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the comply-now trap: AIDA died at the January 2025 prorogation and no successor text exists to comply WITH — building conformity machinery against a rumour misallocates capital. Voluntarily adopting good practice differs from (c)'s pretence that EU law maps onto a nonexistent Canadian statute.

ii-rr-ca-s01.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the still-in-committee myth — AIDA (Bill C-27 Part 3) is dead, not dormant, and no successor bill has been tabled as of August 2026. The government has said future AI legislation will proceed separately from privacy reform, so (d) is backwards too.

ii-rr-ca-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the ADM Directive is genuinely binding, but only on the federal government's own decision systems, so it sets no private-sector expectations. PIPEDA has no AI chapter (c), and no province has a general private-sector AI act (d) — Ontario's 2024 act reaches only public-sector use.

ii-rr-ch-c01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the decision expressly REJECTED a horizontal act in favour of the lean sectoral route — the opposite of the EU's choice next door. (d) mistakes Switzerland's institutional position: it is not in the EEA and has no mechanism to adopt the AI Act wholesale.

ii-rr-ch-c02.why: Nearest confusable is (b), the classic 'no AI law means no law' error — the FADP, product rules and financial supervision all reach AI systems today. (c) is wrong on mechanism: EU rules are not Swiss law and bite only extraterritorially where output is used in the EU market.

ii-rr-ch-s01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Switzerland is neither EU nor EEA, so the AI Act is not Swiss law — though it can still reach a Swiss firm extraterritorially when output is used in the EU. (d) fails on status: Switzerland SIGNED the Convention in March 2025 but has not ratified it.

ii-rr-ch-s02.why: Nearest confusable is (b): that is the UNITED KINGDOM'S position — the UK ratified and the Convention has been in force for it since 2025-11-01. Switzerland is a signatory only, and a treaty of this kind needs ratification plus implementing legislation before it binds (contra d).

ii-rr-cn-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b): what took effect on 2026-01-01 is the amended Cybersecurity Law with AI safe-development provisions — not a comprehensive AI statute. (c) confuses China with Japan or Singapore: China's measures are fully binding, just not consolidated.

ii-rr-cn-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the State Council's 'accelerate comprehensive legislation' commitment is a drafting agenda, not an enactment — no unified statute is in force as of 2026-08-02. The CSL amendment (adopted by the NPC Standing Committee 2025-10-28) is real but is an amendment to existing law, not the awaited AI act.

ii-rr-cn-n01.why: The nearest confusable is (b): data localisation is a Cybersecurity Law / Data Security Law concern — the Interim Measures' training-data governance duty is about source legality, IP and personal-information compliance, and training data is expressly in scope (contrary to (c)).

ii-rr-cn-n02.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which describes Korea's operator-only duty design — China uniquely extends verification and re-labelling duties to distribution platforms. Implicit metadata labels are mandatory, not optional, so (c) fails too.

ii-rr-cn-p01.why: The nearest confusable is (b): no unified AI statute exists in China as of August 2026 — comprehensive-law drafting has only been accelerated on the 2026 legislative agenda. (c) adds AI safe-development language but is not the operative service-level rulebook; (d) is Singapore's voluntary framework. The Interim Measures have been in force since 2023-08-15.

ii-rr-cn-p02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): self-assessment-plus-marking is the EU internal-control conformity route — China's mechanism is administrative filing in a regulator-run registry (Algorithm Recommendation Provisions, in force 2022-03-01), and public-facing generative services file too: 796 had completed filing as of 2026-02-28. Filing is not certification and not CE marking.

ii-rr-cn-p03.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the layering is the tested fact — China stacks instruments rather than replacing them, so the Deep Synthesis Provisions (eff. 2023-01-10) operate alongside the Labelling Measures and GB 45438-2025. Assuming the newer measure supersedes the older is the classic error in this regime.

ii-rr-cn-p04.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the realistic-vs-clearly-artificial distinction is Korea's rule under its Framework Act — China requires BOTH label types on generated output regardless. (d) inverts the duty split: platforms have their own verify-and-relabel obligations, but that supplements rather than replaces the generator's duty.

ii-rr-cn-p05.why: The nearest confusable is (b): third-party conformity assessment is the EU's reserved route for certain biometric systems — China's gate for services with public-opinion attributes is a regulator-facing security assessment paired with filing. (c) is the EU deployer's FRIA; (d) is Singapore's voluntary assurance tooling.

ii-rr-co-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b): no court ever ruled the law unconstitutional — xAI's suit (filed 2026-04-09, DOJ intervening) produced a stay, and the LEGISLATURE then repealed and replaced it. Option (c) erases the litigation pressure that shaped the outcome.

ii-rr-co-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which inverts the outcome — disclosure and transparency are exactly what SB 26-189 KEPT; the heavyweight governance machinery is what went. That deletion is why commentators describe the replacement as substantially narrower.

ii-rr-co-k01.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the signing-date-equals-effective-date error — SB 26-189 was signed 2026-05-14 but operates from 2027-01-01. Option (b) treats a dead law as live. Colorado today is a gap: general consumer and privacy law apply, nothing AI-specific.

ii-rr-co-s01.why: The nearest confusables are (b) and (d), which recite the two effective dates that never arrived: 2026-02-01 was pushed to 2026-06-30 by SB 25B-004, and the repeal-and-replace (2026-05-14) landed first. SB 24-205 produced zero days of operative law.

ii-rr-co-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which describes TEXAS's TRAIGA — in force since January 2026 and intent-based. Colorado's SB 26-189 is a disclosure/transparency regime for automated decision technology and does not operate until 2027-01-01.

ii-rr-co-s03.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the developer duty-of-care with impact assessments was the REPEALED SB 24-205 design; SB 26-189 largely eliminated the developer/deployer duty split and weighted what remains toward deployers. Importers (c) are an EU role with no Colorado analogue.

ii-rr-co-s04.why: The nearest confusable is (d) — the DOJ did intervene in the court challenge, but no federal preemption statute exists; the reversal was Colorado's own legislature. Four moves in two years is the date-churn lesson: a compliance date is not a fact you memorise once.

ii-rr-coe-c01.why: Nearest confusable is (c): the FRIA (AI Act Art. 27) is EU law and deployer-facing — HUDERIA is Council of Europe methodology supporting Convention implementation, and it is guidance, not itself mandatory (b). (d) describes ISO/IEC 42001, a different animal entirely.

ii-rr-coe-c02.why: Nearest confusable is (c): signature signals intent — obligations attach only on ratification and entry into force for that party. The US and Japan have signed but not ratified (d), and the treaty is expressly open to non-members (b).

ii-rr-coe-s01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): conformity assessment is EU AI Act machinery — the Convention contains no company-facing operative rules. (d) is the stale fact this game punishes: CETS 225 entered into force on 2025-11-01.

ii-rr-coe-s02.why: Nearest confusable is (c): unlike the OECD Principles or the G7 Hiroshima Process, CETS 225 creates binding obligations for its parties. It is a Council of Europe treaty open to non-members — international, not national (b) — and not an EU act (d): the EU is acceding to it as a party.

ii-rr-coe-s03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the treaty's general entry into force (2025-11-01) bound the states that had ratified by then — for each new party, including the EU, the clock runs from its own ratification, with effect 2026-09-01. (d) borrows the Digital Omnibus deferral date from an entirely different instrument.

ii-rr-eu-c01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Annex III sits a full year later, on 2027-12-02 — 2026-12-02 is the Omnibus's own transition date, closing the Art. 50 watermarking grace for pre-August-2026 systems and switching on the new Art. 5 NCII/CSAM ban it added. (c) is stale by four months — fining powers arrived 2026-08-02; (d) misses both December-2026 items.

ii-rr-eu-c02.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the pre-Omnibus calendar would indeed have made high-risk duties bite today, but Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved Annex III to 2027-12-02. (c) over-corrects in the other direction — GPAI duties and Article 50 are live alongside the prohibitions.

ii-rr-eu-d01.why: Article 26 is the deployer's operational set. Nearest confusables: (b) and (c) are the PROVIDER'S pre-market duties — the deployer inherits neither by merely using the system; (d) is the Article 50 synthetic-content marking duty, which belongs to providers of generative systems.

ii-rr-eu-d02.why: Nearest confusable is (d): that describes the GDPR Article 35 DPIA. The Article 27 FRIA is deployer-side and limited to public-sector-type deployers plus specified credit/insurance uses — not every deployer, and not annual (b); (c) confuses it with the provider's conformity assessment.

ii-rr-eu-d03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Omnibus deferred Annex III high-risk duties, not Article 50, which became enforceable 2026-08-02. (c) names the PROVIDER'S marking duty — the deployer side is deepfake labelling and informing exposed persons; (d) the FRIA is a high-risk instrument for public-sector-type deployers, not a transparency disclosure.

ii-rr-eu-d04.why: Nearest confusable is (b): enabling oversight by design is the PROVIDER'S Article 14 duty; the deployer's Article 26(2) duty is assigning capable people. (c) overstates — oversight means meaningful ability to intervene, not per-output human approval.

ii-rr-eu-i01.why: Nearest confusable is (c): the importer VERIFIES the provider completed the pre-market steps (Art. 23) — it does not redo them. (d) confuses the importer with the authorised representative, a separate mandated role; (b) ignores that importers carry their own verification and identification duties.

ii-rr-eu-i02.why: Nearest confusable is (b): putting your name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market is precisely the Article 25(1)(a) trigger that re-allocates the provider role. (d) is wrong on the mechanism — the original provider owes cooperation and documentation handover, not joint provider status.

ii-rr-eu-i03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the WRITTEN MANDATE to act for a third-country provider is the defining mark of the authorised representative (Art. 22), while the importer is the EU entity that places a third-country system on the market. Neither role attaches by mere position in the chain (c), and neither firm is using the system (d).

ii-rr-eu-k01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Digital Omnibus moved the Annex III date but left the Article 57 sandbox deadline at 2026-08-02. (c) confuses the UK's Regulating for Growth Bill — a proposal before Parliament, and not EU law — with the EU member-state obligation.

ii-rr-eu-n01.why: Nearest confusable is (b): declarations of conformity and CE marking belong to the HIGH-RISK product-safety machinery, not the GPAI chapter. (c) is a deployer instrument; (d) misapplies the Omnibus deferral, which moved Annex III/I dates and left GPAI duties (applying since 2025-08-02) untouched.

ii-rr-eu-n02.why: Nearest confusable is (b): untargeted scraping of facial images is an Article 5 PROHIBITED practice, not an Annex III high-risk use — no conformity route legalises it. (c) fails on currency: the prohibitions applied from 2025-02-02 and were untouched by the Digital Omnibus.

ii-rr-eu-p01.why: Annex III employment systems use the internal-control route (Art. 43(2)) — self-assess, CE-mark, register. Nearest confusable: (b) third-party assessment is for biometrics without fully applied harmonised standards. (c) is the deployer's FRIA; (d) is NYC LL144. High-risk duties bind from 2027-12-02 (Digital Omnibus deferral), which is why the stem is future-dated.

ii-rr-eu-p02.why: The stagger is the tested point and (b) is the nearest confusable: Art. 53 duties applied from 2025-08-02, while the Commission/AI Office enforcement and fining powers (Art. 101) arrive 2026-08-02. (c) is the prohibited-practices band, not the GPAI band; (d) confuses the GPAI chapter with the Annex III deferral.

ii-rr-eu-p03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): deepfake labelling and emotion-recognition disclosure are the DEPLOYER'S Article 50 duties; the provider side is machine-readable marking plus interaction disclosure. (c) misreads the Omnibus — Article 50 became enforceable 2026-08-02 (only a watermarking grace to 2026-12-02 for systems already on the market); (d) is high-risk product machinery, not transparency.

ii-rr-eu-p04.why: Nearest confusable is (b): emotion recognition OUTSIDE workplaces and schools sits in Annex III as high-risk, but in the workplace it is an Article 5 prohibited practice — no conformity route legalises it. (d) misapplies the Omnibus: the deferral touched Annex III, while the prohibitions have applied since 2025-02-02.

ii-rr-eu-p05.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Article 73 serious-incident reporting attaches to HIGH-RISK systems and was deferred with Annex III to 2027-12-02; the systemic-risk GPAI duty (Art. 55, to the AI Office) has applied since 2025-08-02. ii-rr-in-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): that bill is a private member's bill introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2025, not enacted law. The DPDP regime is not AI-specific, but its consent requirements reach personal data used for model training — which is exactly why (c) is wrong.

ii-rr-in-s03.why: The nearest confusable is (c), over-applying India's 'voluntary' label: accurate for the horizontal framework, but the deepfake-labelling rules under the IT Act (Gazette notification February 2026) are binding and AI-specific — user declarations, prominent labels, provenance metadata where feasible. ii-rr-jp-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which is Taiwan's AI Basic Act timeline (passed 2025-12-23, effective 2026-01-14) — the two Asian framework statutes are easy to swap because they share the no-business-duties design.

ii-rr-jp-c02.why: The pattern recurs in Taiwan's Basic Act — statute in force, business duties absent — so 'has an AI law' is never sufficient for a compliance trigger. In Japan the trigger for companies remains general law (APPI, product liability), not the AI statute, and nothing was repealed.

ii-rr-jp-s01.why: The nearest confusable is (d), the outdated claim: Japan HAS a binding statute — the AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025), in force since 2025-06-04 — it just imposes no business obligations. ii-rr-jp-s02.why: The nearest confusable is (b)/(d): the Act does create government machinery — the AI Strategy Headquarters and the AI Basic Plan (adopted by Cabinet 2025-12-23) — but that machinery directs the state, not business. ii-rr-jp-s03.why: The nearest confusable is (b): a 3%-of-turnover fining power is the EU Commission's GPAI enforcement tool — Japan's act contains no monetary penalties at all. Reputational naming after investigation is the only teeth; there is no suspension or recall power in the statute.

ii-rr-ke-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the Commissioner's office does not exist yet — it is created only if the bill passes. The African Union (c) issues continental strategy, not directly applicable regulation. The March 2025 strategy (about KES 152bn) is the operative framework.

ii-rr-ke-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): nothing is enacted — a first-reading bill is precisely what puts Kenya ahead on the dedicated-statute track. ii-rr-ke-s01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the classic proposed-tier trap: Senate Bill No. 4 (published 2026-02-19, first reading 2026-04-02) is at committee stage, not law. (c) gets the criticism right but the withdrawal wrong; (d) understates a real bill before the Senate.

ii-rr-kr-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (c), which transplants the EU's deferred Annex III timeline onto Korea — the Framework Act has applied since 2026-01-22; what is soft-pedalled in 2026 is enforcement, not applicability. ii-rr-kr-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the EU's provider/deployer/importer split allocates sharply different duty sets per role, and Korea rejected that design — its two operator types largely share obligations, and Korea's foreign-operator domestic-representative duty is threshold-based (user/revenue scale) where the EU's authorised-representative duty (Art. 22) is role-based, attaching to every third-country provider.

ii-rr-kr-d01.why: The nearest confusable is (c): Korea's Act attaches its own duty content to the bank's use — safety/reliability measures and protection of the users the model is run on — rather than importing the EU's deployer duty set; the utilization operator sits roughly where the EU deployer does, but the duties come from the Korean statute alone. ii-rr-kr-n03.why: The nearest confusable is (b): an enumerated use-case annex is the EU's Annex III architecture — Korea uses criteria-based determination under the Enforcement Decree, which businesses report remains vague in practice.

ii-rr-tx-p01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — that duty-of-care-plus-impact-assessment design was Colorado's original SB 24-205 model, which TRAIGA deliberately rejected in favor of intent-based prohibitions. Third-party conformity assessment (c) is the EU route; no US state runs one.

ii-rr-uk-s02.why: Nearest confusable is (b): that is the OLD Article 22 posture the Data (Use and Access) Act replaced — UK GDPR Articles 22A–22D flip the default to permission-with-safeguards (human intervention, representations, contest). ii-rr-uk-s03.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the binding duty falls on the REGULATOR — to prepare the code — not directly on companies; the code will then guide enforcement of existing law. (c) is impossible post-Brexit mechanics; nothing in the SI licenses developers (d).
