ii-rr-us-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the EU-style risk-tier model — no US federal statute does that. Provenance labelling (c) is California SB 942's territory, not federal law. The TAKE IT DOWN Act's platform removal process had to be in place by 2026-05-19.

ii-rr-us-n01.why: The nearest confusable is the jurisdiction gambit (b) — Section 5 reaches AI conduct without any AI-specific statute, so that argument loses. Substantiation must pre-date the claim; framework alignment (c) is good hygiene but does not immunize deception.

ii-rr-us-n02.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the human-in-the-loop misconception — ECOA's adverse-action duty attaches to the credit decision however it is made. A generic below-threshold line (b) fails the specificity requirement the CFPB reiterated for AI models.

ii-rr-us-s01.why: The nearest confusable is the TAKE IT DOWN Act — it really is a federal AI statute, but its scope is narrow (non-consensual intimate deepfakes), not comprehensive. The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, and executive orders bind agencies, not companies.

ii-rr-us-s02.why: The nearest confusable is the no-federal-AI-act fallacy: absence of an AI statute is not absence of law — FTC Act §5 already reaches AI-washing. The CFPB's adverse-action rules govern credit decisions, not ad copy, and NIST has no enforcement power at all.

ii-rr-us-s03.why: The nearest confusable is the black-box excuse (b): ECOA/Regulation B require specific reasons and the CFPB has said model complexity is no defense. Handing over documentation or routing to the FTC answers a different question — the duty is a reasons notice to the applicant.

ii-rr-us-s04.why: The nearest confusable is ISO/IEC 42001, which IS a certifiable management-system standard — the NIST AI RMF has no certification scheme and no legal mandate. Option (d) imports the EU notified-body machinery, which belongs to AI Act conformity assessment, not NIST.

ii-rr-us-s05.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which imports the EU's high-risk registration database — the US has no such register. The patchwork discipline is activity-based: CFPB/ECOA for credit, FDA for medical devices, EEOC/Title VII for hiring. Framework profiles (d) are voluntary choices, not jurisdictional facts.

ii-rr-usca-c01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — CE marking is EU conformity iconography with no California analogue. SB 53 is a transparency statute: publish the safety framework, protect whistleblowers, report critical incidents. It licenses nothing and divests nothing (c).

ii-rr-usca-c02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): unlike the EU AI Act's single role taxonomy, California has no unified scheme — AB 2013 names developers, SB 942 covered providers, the CCPA regs businesses. Option (c) describes Colorado's deployer-weighted replacement law, not California.

ii-rr-usca-d01.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — the CRD's FEHA rules also reach automated decisions but only in EMPLOYMENT; lending is a 'significant decision' under the CPPA's ADMT regulations. No federal ADMT framework exists (d), and SB 942 (b) is about content provenance, not decisions.

ii-rr-usca-d02.why: The nearest confusable is (b): SB 942 marks AI-GENERATED CONTENT, while SB 1001 governs conversational identity when a bot incentivizes a sale or influences a vote — different disclosure objects. Option (d) describes Texas TRAIGA, the wrong state.

ii-rr-usca-d03.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the CPPA's ADMT regs also touch employment decisions, but the DISCRIMINATION question runs through the CRD's FEHA rules (effective 2025-10-01). Option (d) is false: those rules are already in force, no waiting period.

ii-rr-usca-n01.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which misreads the phase-in as total deferral — the CPPA regulations have been effective since 2026-01-01; only the significant-decision ADMT compliance deadline runs to 2027-01-01. Option (c) invents an autonomy threshold the rules do not use.

ii-rr-usca-n02.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — the EU AI Act's serious-incident reporting is the parallel mechanism but the wrong jurisdiction; SB 53 routes critical incidents to California's OES. The city consumer-affairs channel (b) is NYC LL144's enforcement home, unrelated to frontier models.

ii-rr-usca-p01.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the training-data summary is AB 2013's separate duty, not SB 942's. SB 942 became operative today (2026-08-02, after the AB 853 delay) for covered providers over one million monthly visitors or users; the bias audit (c) is NYC's mechanism.

ii-rr-usca-p02.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — repeal-and-replace is Colorado's story; California merely DELAYED via AB 853 (chaptered 2025-10-13). No court has enjoined SB 942 (d). The lesson is date-churn: track amendments, not just enactments.

ii-rr-usca-p03.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which overreads AB 2013 — the duty is a high-level summary (sources, types, copyright/personal-data flags), never corpus disclosure. Option (c) imports EU risk-tier gating; AB 2013 applies without any risk classification.

ii-tp-01.a.text: Defines the common vocabulary and conceptual framework for AI — terms like AI system, machine learning, training, inference, and bias — so every other AI standard rests on the same definitions.
ii-tp-01.a.why: This is the dictionary of AI governance: it eliminates ambiguity in technical, legal, and governance discussions by fixing what the words mean, but it imposes no organisational requirements of its own.
ii-tp-01.b.text: Specifies a certifiable AI management system (AIMS) — policies, governance structures, risk controls, and oversight mechanisms an organisation can be independently audited against.
ii-tp-01.b.why: Published 2023, this moves AI governance from voluntary principles to auditable, certifiable practice — the AI-governance equivalent of ISO/IEC 27001 for information security.

ii-tp-02.a.text: Guides how an organisation assesses an AI system's effects on individuals and societies — an AI impact assessment standard.
ii-tp-02.a.why: 42005 scopes the assessment around the people and communities the system touches, not the organisation's internal risk posture.
ii-tp-02.b.text: Guides how an organisation manages AI-related risk across its own processes — risk identification, analysis, evaluation, and treatment.
ii-tp-02.b.why: 23894 is the AI-specific companion to ISO 31000's generic risk-management process, aimed at the organisation's risk function rather than the affected individual.

ii-tp-03.a.text: A marketing bot's ad copy claims the AI hiring tool is 'completely objective'; the system later exhibits bias and the regulator calls the claim deceptive.
ii-tp-03.a.why: The FTC Act bars false or exaggerated claims about what a product can do — the defect here is in what was said about the system, not in the system itself.
ii-tp-03.b.text: A flaw in how the system was engineered means it fails to perform as safely as consumers are entitled to expect, and a user is injured as a result.
ii-tp-03.b.why: Under doctrines like the EU Product Liability Directive, manufacturers can be strictly liable for a defective design even without proof of negligence — the harm traces to engineering, not messaging.

ii-tp-04.a.text: Widely adopted, high-level principles for trustworthy AI — a values-level reference point rather than a step-by-step process.
ii-tp-04.a.why: The OECD's contribution is normative and international: what trustworthy AI should look like, not how to operationalise finding and fixing its risks.
ii-tp-04.b.text: A U.S.-originated but globally influential framework built specifically to help organisations identify and mitigate AI risks in practice.
ii-tp-04.b.why: The RMF is operational scaffolding — functions like Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage — that an organisation actually runs, distinct from OECD's principle-level guidance.

ii-tp-05.a.text: A published summary of a model's data sources, known risks, and mitigations, written in language a non-expert can understand.
ii-tp-05.a.why: A model card documents what the model already is and does — transparency about a finished artefact.
ii-tp-05.b.text: A forward-looking review, carried out before launch, of the harms an AI system might cause and how each will be controlled.
ii-tp-05.b.why: An impact assessment looks forward at consequences for people and society, not backward at what the model card already discloses about the artefact.

ii-tp-06.a.text: The vendor contractually promises the AI model will perform to a stated standard; if it doesn't, the deployer has a contract remedy against the vendor.
ii-tp-06.a.why: A warranty is a promise about the product itself — it fails or holds based on whether the system performs as stated.
ii-tp-06.b.text: The vendor agrees to cover the deployer's losses if a third party sues over IP infringement or a regulatory violation caused by the model — but the clause is voided once the deployer uses the model outside the jurisdictions the vendor covered.
ii-tp-06.b.why: Indemnity reallocates who pays for a third-party claim; it says nothing about whether the model itself works, and — as exam-prep materials note — it can be voided by deploying outside the covered jurisdiction.

ii-tp-07.a.text: A claimant must show the developer failed to exercise reasonable care in designing, testing, or validating the system before liability attaches.
ii-tp-07.a.why: Negligence liability turns on proving a failure of care — no proof of fault, no claim.
ii-tp-07.b.text: Under the EU Product Liability Directive, a manufacturer can be held liable for damage caused by a defective AI-enabled product even without any proof of negligence.
ii-tp-07.b.why: Strict liability removes the fault question entirely: if the product was defective and caused harm, liability can attach regardless of how carefully the manufacturer behaved.

ii-tp-08.a.text: An AI diagnostic tool that processes protected health information must comply with privacy and security rules covering access controls, audit logs, and breach notification.
ii-tp-08.a.why: HIPAA's obligations attach the moment protected health information is processed, regardless of whether a decision is even automated.
ii-tp-08.b.text: An AI model that denies a consumer a loan must provide an adverse-action notice explaining the key factors driving the decision, and the underlying credit-scoring model must not produce discriminatory outcomes.
ii-tp-08.b.why: These finance-sector laws require explainability and non-discrimination specifically for credit decisions — a different duty, in a different sector, from HIPAA's data-handling rules.

importer.definition: Established in the EU and places on the market a system bearing the name or trademark of a third-country entity.

joint.definition: Two or more controllers that jointly determine purposes and means.

map-ae.tell: Binding AI rules live only inside a financial free zone — the scope of the sectoral rule is a place, not an industry.

map-au.tell: The 2024 mandatory-guardrails proposal was abandoned in the December 2025 National AI Plan — Australia chose to stay voluntary, not to drift toward binding rules.

map-br.tell: Stalled, not abandoned. Meanwhile the data protection law does the work.

map-ca.tell: A high-value distractor: AIDA is dead — it died on the order paper in January 2025 and was never revived — yet it is still widely cited as pending.

map-ch.tell: The deliberate minimalist — a lean, sector-specific approach chosen on purpose, next door to the EU's comprehensive regime.

map-cn.tell: A stack of binding measures rather than one statute, and the only major regime built around content control and filing.

map-coe.tell: International instrument, not a national law — in force and binding, but on states: companies feel it only through national implementation.

map-eu.tell: The only regime combining a risk tier system with product-safety machinery (CE marking, notified bodies, conformity assessment).

map-in.tell: Large AI market with an official voluntary framework — MeitY guidelines plus a phasing data-protection regime, still no comprehensive AI statute.

map-jp.tell: A binding statute with no business duties or penalties — the counterexample that shows 'has an AI law' does not mean 'has AI obligations'.

map-ke.tell: Africa's strongest legislative candidate — a licensing-commissioner model, not an EU-style provider/deployer chain.

map-kr.tell: Second comprehensive AI law in force worldwide. Named in BoK v2.1 but absent from the study guide — the domestic-representative duty has no EU AI Act equivalent.

map-pe.tell: First binding general AI framework in force in Latin America — promotion-oriented and lighter than the EU, while Brazil's bill is still pending.

map-sg.tell: The voluntary exemplar — world's first governance framework specifically for agentic AI, and still nothing AI-specific is enforceable.

map-tw.tell: The Japan pattern repeated: a binding framework statute in force with no business duties — obligations arrive only via forthcoming risk-classification and sectoral rules.

map-uk.tell: Principles delegated to existing regulators rather than a new statute.

map-us.tell: Regulation by existing statute and enforcement, not by a new AI act.

map-us-ca.tell: Closest US analogue to GDPR-style ADM rights.

map-us-co.tell: Four moves in two years. The clearest proof that a compliance date is not a fact you memorise once.

map-us-il.tell: Amends existing civil rights law rather than creating a new AI regime.

map-us-nyc.tell: Earliest operative AI hiring rule anywhere, and city-level — jurisdiction is not only national.

map-us-tx.tell: The third state comprehensive AI law — cross-sector but light-touch and intent-based, unlike Colorado's effects-based consequential-decision model.

processor.definition: Processes personal data on behalf of the controller.

provider.definition: Develops an AI system or has one developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark.

roles-aiact.obligations[2].text: Carry out the conformity assessment and affix CE marking

roles-aiact.obligations[5].text: Design the system so human oversight is possible
roles-aiact.obligations[6].text: Apply data governance to training, validation and test data
roles-aiact.obligations[7].text: Conduct post-market monitoring and report serious incidents
roles-aiact.obligations[8].text: Use the system in accordance with the instructions for use
roles-aiact.obligations[9].text: Assign human oversight to people with the competence and authority to act
roles-aiact.obligations[10].text: Ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose
roles-aiact.obligations[11].text: Inform workers and their representatives before putting a high-risk system into use in the workplace
roles-aiact.obligations[12].text: Inform individuals that they are subject to a high-risk system's decision
roles-aiact.obligations[13].text: Retain automatically generated logs for the required period
roles-aiact.obligations[14].text: Carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment where required
roles-aiact.obligations[15].text: Verify the provider has completed the conformity assessment before placing on the market
roles-aiact.obligations[16].text: Verify the third-country provider has appointed an authorised representative
roles-aiact.obligations[17].text: Indicate your name and contact address on the system or its packaging

roles-aiact.obligations[21].text: Terminate the mandate if the provider acts contrary to its obligations, and inform the authority

roles-gdpr.obligations[0].text: Identify a lawful basis before processing begins
roles-gdpr.obligations[1].text: Provide Article 13 and 14 transparency information to data subjects
roles-gdpr.obligations[2].text: Respond to access, rectification, erasure and objection requests
roles-gdpr.obligations[3].text: Carry out a data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing
roles-gdpr.obligations[4].text: Notify the supervisory authority of a breach within 72 hours
roles-gdpr.obligations[5].text: Communicate a high-risk breach to affected data subjects
roles-gdpr.obligations[6].text: Put an Article 28 contract in place before engaging a processor
roles-gdpr.obligations[7].text: Establish a transfer mechanism under Chapter V before sending data abroad
roles-gdpr.obligations[8].text: Agree an arrangement setting out respective responsibilities, and make its essence available to data subjects
roles-gdpr.obligations[9].text: Accept that a data subject may exercise their rights against either of you, regardless of the arrangement
roles-gdpr.obligations[10].text: Process only on documented instructions from the controller
roles-gdpr.obligations[11].text: Obtain authorisation before engaging a sub-processor
roles-gdpr.obligations[12].text: Notify the controller of a personal data breach without undue delay
roles-gdpr.obligations[13].text: Assist the controller in responding to data subject requests
roles-gdpr.obligations[14].text: Delete or return the data at the end of the engagement
roles-gdpr.obligations[15].text: Inform and advise on obligations, and monitor compliance, without receiving instructions on how to perform the task
roles-gdpr.obligations[16].text: Act as the contact point for the supervisory authority and for data subjects
roles-gdpr.obligations[17].text: Maintain the record of processing activities and make it available to the authority on request

roles-overlap.prompt: For each statement, decide whether it belongs to the EU AI Act, the GDPR, or both.
roles-overlap.items[0].text: Roles are assigned by who places a system on the market or puts it into service
roles-overlap.items[0].why: Market placement is the AI Act's allocator. The GDPR allocates by who determines purposes and means.
roles-overlap.items[1].text: Roles are assigned by who determines the purposes and means of processing
roles-overlap.items[2].text: An organisation can be a provider under one regime and a controller under the other for the same system
roles-overlap.items[2].why: The two role sets are independent. A provider may process no personal data at all; a deployer is very often the controller.
roles-overlap.items[3].text: Requires an impact assessment before high-risk activity
roles-overlap.items[3].why: AI Act fundamental rights impact assessment for certain deployers; GDPR Article 35 DPIA for high-risk processing. Different triggers, different scopes, and they can be run together.
roles-overlap.items[4].text: Gives an individual the right not to be subject to a solely automated decision with significant effects
roles-overlap.items[4].why: Article 22 is a data subject right. The AI Act imposes oversight duties on organisations but does not create this right.
roles-overlap.items[5].text: Obliges providers and deployers to tell people that the system they are dealing with is an AI
roles-overlap.items[5].why: Article 50 transparency. GDPR notice obligations are about processing of personal data, which is a different subject matter.
roles-overlap.items[6].text: Applies to organisations outside the EU on the basis of effects inside it
roles-overlap.items[6].why: Both reach extraterritorially, but on different triggers: market placement or output used in the EU, versus establishment, offering goods and services, or monitoring behaviour.
roles-overlap.items[7].text: Maximum fines can reach 7% of total worldwide annual turnover
roles-overlap.items[7].why: The Article 5 prohibitions band. The GDPR tops out at 4% or €20 million.
roles-overlap.items[8].text: Permits processing special categories of data specifically to detect and correct bias, subject to safeguards
roles-overlap.items[8].why: AI Act Article 10(5) creates the permission for high-risk bias monitoring; it has to be read with GDPR Article 9. Neither works alone.
roles-overlap.items[9].why: The AI Act is enforced by market surveillance authorities and the AI Office — though some member states have designated their DPA as the market surveillance authority for certain Annex III areas.
roles-overlap.items[10].text: Requires data used for training to be relevant, representative and as free of errors as possible
roles-overlap.items[10].why: Article 10 data governance for high-risk systems. This sits in genuine tension with GDPR data minimisation, and reconciling the two is a governance judgment, not a lookup.
roles-overlap.items[11].text: Requires records to be kept that demonstrate compliance
roles-overlap.items[11].why: AI Act technical documentation, logging and record-keeping; GDPR Article 30 records and the Article 5(2) accountability principle.
roles-overlap.items[12].text: Obligations can attach to you even if you never touch personal data
roles-overlap.items[12].why: A provider of a high-risk system processing only industrial sensor data still carries the full obligation set. This is the cleanest demonstration that the two regimes are not nested.

tl-au-001.note: Apply privacy-impact, consumer-protection, safety and sectoral controls today; track proposed guardrails.

tl-au-002.note: Prepare accountability, testing, data-governance, transparency and contestability controls; dates unconfirmed.

tl-br-001.note: Build privacy, automated-decision explanation and data-governance evidence; monitor the AI bill.

tl-br-002.note: Prepare EU-style risk classification, governance and impact-assessment capability; enactment date uncertain.

tl-ca-002.note: Monitor a replacement legislative vehicle; do not base compliance dates on AIDA.

tl-cn-001.note: Assess filing/security-assessment exposure, content controls, user identity and provenance labelling.

tl-eu-001.note: Article 5 bans and Article 4 AI-literacy duties; maintain screening and training evidence.

tl-eu-002.note: Technical documentation, training-content summary, copyright-policy and systemic-risk evidence for GPAI providers.

tl-eu-004.note: Complete AI inventory/classification and assign provider/deployer/importer/distributor roles.

tl-eu-007.note: A regulatory-support milestone, not a direct company deadline — use as a benchmark for frontier/GPAI governance.

tl-eu-008.note: Secure-by-design, vulnerability-management, technical documentation, conformity and lifecycle support.

tl-eu-010.milestone: Annex I high-risk systems embedded in regulated products apply
tl-eu-010.note: Integrate AI Act evidence with CE marking, product safety, quality management and post-market surveillance. Postponed from 2 Aug 2027 to this date by the Amendments Regulation (the "Digital Omnibus").

tl-in-001.note: Apply consent/data controls and content/intermediary obligations; monitor AI governance proposals.

tl-jp-001.note: Documented risk management, data governance, transparency and sector-specific assessments.

tl-kr-001.note: AI inventory, high-impact use-case assessment, transparency, safety and human-oversight controls; check extraterritorial reach.

tl-my-001.note: AI-system inventory, privacy/data controls, cyber incident workflows and content-risk procedures.

tl-my-002.note: Build readiness for lifecycle roles, risk tiering, incident reporting and central-authority oversight.

tl-sa-gcc-001.note: Map localisation, cross-border transfer, cloud assurance and critical-infrastructure requirements before deployment.

tl-sg-001.note: AI Verify-style testing, model documentation and assurance evidence for government/enterprise buyers.

tl-uae-002.note: Monitor federal ministries, the UAE AI Office, CBUAE, DFSA, FSRA, VARA, DIFC and ADGM per footprint.

tl-uk-001.note: Map each use case to sector, privacy, equality, consumer and online-safety obligations; watch regulator guidance.

tl-us-ca-001.note: Public AI disclosures and training-data/governance evidence where the law applies.
